The Brazilian damsel (Stegastes fuscus) is a common territorial damselfish inhabiting rocky reefs along the southwestern Atlantic coast. Newly hatched larvae emerge from demersal eggs after an incubation period of approximately six days [ab = approximately six days] at the ambient seawater temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. These prolarvae are lecithotrophic, relying on endogenous yolk reserves during the initial phase of larval life. At the moment of hatching, each newly emerged larva has a wet weight of about 0.00052 grams [Wwb = about 0.00052 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of one millimeter observed in this species. The minute body mass at this stage reflects the limited yolk provisioning that characterizes the small, pelagic eggs of many pomacentrids. This initial endowment must sustain the yolk-sac larva through the brief endotrophic period until the mouth opens and the transition to first exogenous feeding begins.

As the free-swimming larvae grow and develop within the ichthyoplankton, they undergo substantial morphological changes before settling onto the reef. Field surveys indicate that the onset of sexual maturity is tightly linked to body size rather than chronological age alone. Individuals typically reach puberty at a standard length of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters], a milestone that corresponds to a substantial investment in somatic growth. At this size, the wet weight of a maturing individual is approximately 5.4 grams [Wwp = approximately 5.4 grams], reflecting the accumulation of muscle and skeletal tissue necessary for successful territory establishment and spawning. The transition from a pelagic larva to a benthic juvenile involves a dramatic metamorphic climax that includes fin ray ossification and scale formation, preparing the young fish for its demersal lifestyle.

Reproductive adults of Stegastes fuscus exhibit a very high fecundity, a strategy common among reef fishes that produce large numbers of small pelagic eggs. During the peak of the breeding season at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], a single female can produce up to one hundred and twenty-five eggs per day [Ri = up to one hundred and twenty-five eggs per day], a rate that is among the highest recorded for damselfishes of comparable body size. This estimate, drawn from observations of the congeneric Chromis chromis, highlights the potential for rapid population turnover when environmental conditions are favorable. The maximum standard length attained by this species is 12.6 centimeters [Li = 12.6 centimeters], and an individual of this size will have grown to an ultimate wet weight of approximately 32 grams [Wwi = approximately 32 grams]. The males of this species are nest-guarding adults that aerate and defend the adhesive egg clutches laid on the rocky substrate.

The longevity of the Brazilian damsel has been documented through mark-recapture studies conducted on coastal reefs in southeastern Brazil. At a constant water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan reaches 16 years [am = 16 years], which is unusually long for a relatively small-bodied pomacentrid. This extended life history likely reflects the low natural mortality rates experienced by territorial reef fishes that benefit from stable shelter sites and a consistent algal food supply. Senescent adults may show reduced vigor during competition for prime territories, but the overall age structure of populations suggests that physiological deterioration is slow. The body plan reorganization during the larval-juvenile transition is complete well before the adult stage, and growth continues asymptotically toward the maximum standard length.

An evaluation of the life-history traits of Stegastes fuscus reveals a pattern consistent with an iteroparous, late-maturing species that invests heavily in a long reproductive lifespan. The substantial difference in wet weight between a 0.00052 gram [Wwb = 0.00052 gram] hatchling and a 32 gram [Wwi = 32 gram] adult reflects a remarkable growth increment, achieved through a prolonged juvenile phase. At puberty, the standard length of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters] and the corresponding wet weight of 5.4 grams [Wwp = 5.4 grams] indicate that individuals delay reproduction until they have reached approximately 56 percent of their ultimate length, a strategy that likely enhances fecundity once breeding commences. Under the thermal regime of the southwestern Atlantic, the daily egg production of 125 eggs per day [Ri = 125 eggs per day] at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C] is sustained over several months during the warm season, contributing to recruitment pulses that replenish local populations. The oldest individuals in a cohort are routinely observed living for 16 years [am = 16 years], providing multiple breeding seasons over a long lifetime at a temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C].
